title: Line Integrals in Mechanics
short_intro: A line integral in mechanics evaluates the accumulation of a vector or scalar field along a specified curve in space. It is fundamental for determining physical quantities such as work done by a force and the potential energy associated with conservative fields.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Evaluation of line integrals for constant and straightforward position-dependent forces along straight-line paths or simple coordinate axes in Cartesian coordinates.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Computation of work along arbitrary spatial paths, testing for path independence, identifying conservative force fields via curl conditions (∇ × F = 0), and deriving scalar potential functions.

prerequisites: Vector algebra (dot product and cross product)
Parametric representation of curves in 2D and 3D space

concept_notes.heading: Definition of Work Line Integral
bullets: The line integral of a vector force field F along a smooth directed curve C from point A to B is defined as the integral of the tangential component of F along C.
It physically represents the mechanical work done by the force in moving a particle along the path C.
In SI units, it is measured in Joules (J) or kg m² s².

concept_notes.heading: Conservative Forces and Path Independence
bullets: A force field is conservative if the line integral around any closed loop is identically zero.
For conservative forces, the line integral between two points is independent of the path taken and depends only on the initial and final positions.
Examples include the gravitational force and electrostatic force, closely linked to central force problems in mechanics.

concept_notes.heading: Relation to Potential Energy
bullets: The change in potential energy ΔU between two points is defined as the negative of the work done by the conservative force along any path connecting them.
Mathematically, F = -∇U, establishing that the force is the negative gradient of the scalar potential field.
This concept reduces the complexity of mechanical problems by utilizing scalar energy conservation instead of vector equations of motion.

concept_notes.heading: Non-Conservative Forces (e.g., Friction and Coriolis Force)
bullets: Forces for which the line integral along a closed path is non-zero are classified as non-conservative.
Friction dissipates mechanical energy, making the line integral path-dependent.
The Coriolis force, arising in non-inertial rotating frames, performs zero work instantaneously because it is always perpendicular to the velocity vector (F · v = 0).

derivations.title: Work Done by a Uniform Gravitational Force
derivations.conditions: Particle moves from height y_1 to y_2 in a uniform gravitational field g near the Earth's surface.
steps: Express the gravitational force vector as F = -mg j^.
Express the infinitesimal displacement vector along an arbitrary path as dr = dx i^ + dy j^ + dz k^.
Set up the line integral: W = \int_{A}^{B} F \cdot dr = \int_{y_1}^{y_2} (-mg j^) \cdot (dx i^ + dy j^ + dz k^).
Evaluate the dot product: W = \int_{y_1}^{y_2} -mg dy.
Integrate with respect to y to obtain the final result: W = -mg(y_2 - y_1).
derivations.result: W = -\Delta U, where \Delta U = mg(y_2 - y_1)

derivations.title: Condition for Path Independence (Conservative Field)
derivations.conditions: Force field F is continuously differentiable in a simply connected domain.
steps: State the requirement that the line integral around any closed loop C is zero: \oint_{C} F \cdot dr = 0.
Apply Stokes' theorem to convert the closed line integral into a surface integral: \iint_{S} (\nabla \times F) \cdot dS = 0.
Argue that since this holds for any arbitrary surface S bounded by C, the integrand must vanish everywhere in the domain.
derivations.result: \nabla \times F = 0 (Curl of the force field is zero)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Path Independence vs Path Dependence
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two points A and B in the xy-plane connected by multiple distinct paths C_1, C_2, and a closed loop formed by C_1 and C_2 combined.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: For conservative fields, the line integral value is identical along C_1 and C_2. For non-conservative fields (like friction), the integrals differ, and the net loop integral is non-zero.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT to identify conservative fields and mathematically in PGT using vector identities.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force vs Displacement (Central Force)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing gravitational force magnitude f(r) = -GMm/r² plotted against radial distance r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area under the force-displacement curve between r_1 and r_2 represents the work done by the central force, corresponding to the line integral evaluation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical problem visualization for escape velocity and orbital energy.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Work Done by Variable Force Along Straight Line
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of F_x versus x with an arbitrary curve, partitioned into vertical strips of width dx.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the Riemann sum concept that forms the foundation of the 1D line integral.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core concept foundation for TGT mechanics problems.

solved_numericals.question: Find the work done by a constant force F = 2 i^ + 3 j^ N in displacing a particle from position r_1 = i^ - j^ m to r_2 = 3 i^ + 2 j^ m.
solution_steps: Determine the displacement vector dr = r_2 - r_1.
Calculate the line integral / work done: W = F \cdot dr = (2)(2) + (3)(3).

solved_numericals.question: Evaluate the line integral W = \int_{C} (3x^2 dx + 2y dy), where C is the parabola y = x^2 from the origin (0,0) to the point (1,1).
solution_steps: Parameterize the curve using x = t, which gives y = t^2.
Determine differentials: dx = dt and dy = 2t dt.
Set the limits for parameter t from t = 0 to t = 1.
Substitute into the integral: \int_{0}^{1} [3(t^2)(dt) + 2(t^2)(2t dt)] = \int_{0}^{1} (3t^2 + 4t^3) dt.

solved_numericals.question: Show that the force field F = (2xy + z^3) i^ + (x^2) j^ + (3xz^2) k^ is conservative and find the scalar potential U such that F = -\nabla U.
solution_steps: Compute the curl of F: \nabla \times F = \left| \begin{matrix} i^ & j^ & k^ \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ 2xy+z^3 & x^2 & 3xz^2 \end{matrix} \right|.
Evaluate components: i^ (0 - 0) - j^ (3z^2 - 3z^2) + k^ (2x - 2x) = 0 i^ + 0 j^ + 0 k^.
Since \nabla \times F = 0, the force is conservative.
Set - \frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = 2xy + z^3, - \frac{\partial U}{\partial y} = x^2, and - \frac{\partial U}{\partial z} = 3xz^2.
Integrate partial derivatives to find U(x,y,z) = -x^2 y - xz^3 + constant.
solved_numericals.answer: Conservative field with potential U = -x^2 y - xz^3

assumptions_and_limitations: Line integrals in classical mechanics assume macroscopic particles where quantum fluctuations of position and momentum are negligible.
Paths of integration are assumed to be continuous and piecewise smooth in standard coordinate systems.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The line integral of any force field between two points is independent of the path.
common_misconceptions.correct: Path independence holds exclusively for conservative force fields.
common_misconceptions.why: Non-conservative forces like friction depend heavily on the specific trajectory taken.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Coriolis force does work on a particle in a rotating frame because it appears in the equation of motion.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Coriolis force does zero work on a particle.
common_misconceptions.why: The Coriolis force is always perpendicular to the velocity vector of the particle (F_c \cdot v = 0), yielding zero incremental work.

quick_revision: Work done by a force is the line integral W = \int C F \cdot dr.
A force is conservative if and only if its curl is zero (\nabla \times F = 0).
Conservative forces allow the definition of potential energy: \Delta U = -W.
The line integral around any closed loop in a conservative field is zero.
